newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony joins league of DVD makers with March launch.
newsitem.headline: Sony joins league of DVD makers with March launch.

text.p: Sony on Thursday became the last major Japanese manufacturer to launch a high-capacity digital video disc (DVD) system, unveiling the hardware it will sell in Japan from March and the United States from April.
The DVD player, called the DVP-S7000, will be priced at 110,000 yen ($950). The unit can play back DVD video software as well as music and video compact discs.
The players will be on sale in Europe in the middle of 1997, and will be introduced to the rest of Asia some time after the introduction to the U.S. market, Sony said.

A DVD looks like a compact disc (CD) but stores much more information, allowing them to hold feature-length movies, music and other information. A DVD can be played on a computer, or on a player much like today's video cassette recorders.
Industry experts expect the DVD system to eventually replace video movies, CDs and CD-ROMs.
Sony plans to start selling a DVD-ROM drive, a device to play a DVD on a computer, sometime in the next few months in Japan and in April in the U.S.

Rivals like Toshiba Corp and Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd launched their DVD hardware last November, but Sony said it would not introduce its products until spring as there would be few software titles available.
Sony, famed for its innovation and new products, was uncharacteristically cautious on the DVD launch, saying it expected initial sales of DVD machines to be slow.
A group of the world's top 10 electronics and film makers who developed the DVD format had originally pushed for sales to start last summer in Japan.

But tangled negotiations with Hollywood studios over a controversial "copyguard" system designed to prevent users from copying the discs on to other discs or to videotape delayed the debut for months.

Finally last October, entertainment, electronics and computer industry executives reached an agreement on copyright protection issues, removing the huge issue of piracy from the new digitally formatted music and movies.
Indeed, when Toshiba and Matsushita introduced their products to the world in November, there were hardly any software titles were available, industry analysts said.
Toshiba delayed its U.S. launch of its DVD players to January or February because of a lack of software titles.

Analysts agree that though the potential of the DVD system is huge, it will take a few years for the market to take off as the variety and quality of the software titles will be the key to its growth.
